summary: Defines an SMIv2 MIB module for configuring the security policy database of a device that implements IPsec. Its policy-based filtering and actions are general enough to be used beyond IPsec.

plainLanguage.summary: A security guard follows a rulebook for which packets to protect, allow or drop. This defines a standard list of settings to write and read that rulebook remotely.

subtitle: A standard SNMP table set for writing the rulebook that tells an IPsec device which packets to accept, drop or protect.

tldr.problem: An IPsec device needs a security policy database that says what to do with each packet, and administrators need a standard way to configure it remotely.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB module whose tables link filters to actions, group those rules in priority order, and attach each group to an interface and direction.
tldr.outcome: The filters and actions are general enough to configure other packet-handling devices such as a firewall, and further actions can be added through extension MIBs.

facts.label: Static actions
facts.value: 4 (drop, accept, each with or without logging)

today: RFC 4807 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text bases the model on RFC 2401 even though RFC 4301 had already updated that document.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4807 defines a MIB module (a set of managed objects, normally reached through SNMP) for configuring the security policy database (SPD) of a device that implements IPsec. The model it configures comes from the IPsec Configuration Policy Model in RFC 3585, which itself derives from the DMTF IPsec model and from RFC 2401.

The RFC notes that RFC 4301 has updated RFC 2401, but this MIB is still based on RFC 2401. The IPsec-specific and IKE-specific actions are not defined here. They live in companion documents.

The packet filtering and action execution are described as more general than IPsec alone, for example for configuring a firewall.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a form for writing down the rules a network guard follows. It was made for IPsec guards, but it could work for other kinds of guards too.

sections.title: Relationship to the DMTF Policy Model
sections.content:
The MIB is a task-specific SMIv2 version of the IPsec Configuration Policy Model, intended for use with SNMPv3. It departs from that model in two main ways.

  • Policies, groups, conditions and some levels of actions have generic names, without prefixes such as SA or IPsec. Packet classification is more general than IPsec, so other packet-transforming actions could reuse the tables.
  • Filters are more generic and scalable. Instead of the condition/filtering pairing and its restrictions, the MIB offers a compound filter object for complex filters.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors took an existing plan for IPsec rules and made it more flexible, so the same form can be used for other kinds of packet rules.

sections.title: Rules, Filters and Actions
sections.content:
The module is split into rules, filters and actions. Each row of the spdRuleDefinitionTable connects one filter to one action. The rule's filter column can point to a spdCompoundFilterTable row to mean a set of filters, and its action column can point to a spdCompoundActionTable row to mean several actions.

Filters include spdTrueFilter (always true), spdIpHeaderFilterTable, spdIpOffsetFilterTable, spdTimeFilterTable and spdIpsoHeaderFilterTable. The actions defined here are only the simple static ones: spdDropAction, spdDropActionLog, spdAcceptAction and spdAcceptActionLog. The first of each pair is for no logging, the second for logging.

A rule also has a spdRuleDefFilterNegated column that flips the filter result, and an administrative status that can disable it.

Extension action MIBs may impose extra limits on this MIB and may support only a subset of its options.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule says: if the packet looks like this, do that. Filters describe what a packet looks like, and actions are things like let it through or throw it away.

sections.title: Groups, Compound Filters and Recursion
sections.content:
Several tables use recursion. A row in the spdGroupContentsTable names either a rule or another group, so a group can contain rules and sub-groups, with no inherent MIB limit on nesting depth.

A compound filter is a row in spdCompoundFilterTable plus the ordered rows in spdSubfiltersTable that share its name. Its logic type is and or or: with AND all sub-filters must be true, with OR at least one must be. Sub-filters may point to other compound filters. Compound actions work the same way through spdCompoundActionTable and spdSubactionsTable.

Rows of a group are processed from the lowest spdGroupContPriority to the highest, a value from 0 to 65535. Once an action runs for a row, processing of further rows in that group MUST stop.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules can be put in folders, and folders can hold other folders. The guard checks the rules in order and stops at the first one that applies.

sections.title: Applying Policy to Interfaces
sections.content:
The spdEndpointToGroupTable maps an interface to a rule group, with one group per direction (ingress and egress). If an endpoint has a group but no rule in it matches a packet, the default action SHALL be to drop the packet.

If an endpoint has no group, the system-wide groups named by spdIngressPolicyGroupName and spdEgressPolicyGroupName MUST be used. A zero-length name means no system-wide policy exists, and the default of drop SHOULD be executed until one is set.

The RFC walks through an example: on the interface with address 192.0.2.1, drop all traffic from host 192.0.2.6 and accept everything else. It creates a filter for the host, a drop rule using it, an accept-all rule using spdTrueFilter, puts the drop rule in the group at priority 1000 and the accept-all rule at 65535, and attaches the group to the interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Each door of the building gets its own rulebook. If nothing in the book matches a visitor, the guard turns them away.

sections.title: Extending the Module
sections.content:
The MIB is built for reuse. Companion documents define IPsec-specific and IKE-specific actions that plug into the same rule tables. A rule's filter pointer can reference diffServMultiFieldClfrTable from the DiffServ MIB, and implementations MAY support other filter tables or scalars as well.

If a pointer names a non-existent row in a supported table, inconsistentName MUST be returned on the set. If a rule refers to something missing or unsupported during packet processing, the packet MUST be dropped.

The module reserves the spdActions subtree for further actions, which IANA assigns under a documented specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has blank space for new kinds of rules, so people can add new things the guard knows how to do later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because this MIB configures network security, anyone with SET access to it can break that security. Only authenticated administrators with the right access SHOULD configure a device, and only authorized administrators SHOULD read the data, since it could reveal misconfigurations.

The RFC says SNMP versions before SNMPv3 do not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementers are advised to use SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy.

Keying information, other than public keys, MUST NOT be observable by third parties. This includes IKE pre-shared keys. The privacy algorithm used for configuration SHOULD be at least as strong as the IPsec policy being configured. A default SNMPv3 user and password, if a device ships with one, SHOULD be changed or removed.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook is very secret and only the real boss may change it. Sending changes over an unlocked line would be like shouting the guard's orders across the street.

items.title: spdDropAction
items.text: Packet MUST be dropped; SHOULD NOT be logged.

items.text: Packet MUST be dropped; SHOULD be logged.
